title: The Sandwich Photo
text: Your partner texts a photo of their lunch. A sandwich, eaten with two hands, sitting down, in a room with a door. "How's your day? 😊"

choices.label: Reply with a photo of the toddler in a colander

outcomes.text: Staging it takes ten minutes and a bribe. They reply with fourteen crying-laughing faces. For a second, you're on the same team.
Sent. It feels incredible for four seconds. Then three dots appear, disappear, and never come back.

choices.label: Don't reply. Eat crusts over the sink.

outcomes.text: You eat four crusts and half a cheese stick, standing up. A feast. They'll see "Read 12:14" and wonder.

title: Who's More Tired
text: "So tired today 😩," your partner texts at 2:12 PM. You have been awake since 5:14. You have many thoughts, and all of them are numbers.

outcomes.text: It costs you something to send it. They reply with a heart and "you too, I know you're wiped." That costs them something too.

choices.label: Send your wake time, step count and a photo of the ceiling

outcomes.text: 5:14 AM, 11,402 steps and yogurt on the ceiling. Undefeated. They don't reply. You've won, and you're alone with the trophy.
A handshake emoji arrives. 🤝 It isn't a hug, but it isn't a scoreboard either.

title: The Scoreboard
text: "I did bath last night," your partner texts, unprompted, in response to nothing. The scoreboard is open. Someone is keeping it.

outcomes.text: "Thank you" takes you nine tries to type without an edge. It lands. "I just wanted you to know," they write. They did.

choices.label: "And I did the last four mornings."

outcomes.text: "Wasn't a competition." "Then why did you bring it up?" You both put your phones face-down, in different buildings, at the same time.
They scroll. They go quiet. "Okay. Tonight's mine." You were right, which is less fun than it sounds.
They scroll. It's even. Actually, it leans their way. "Interesting document," they reply. You delete the ledger app, then reinstall it.

title: Unprompted
text: Your partner texts, out of nowhere: "You're doing a great job. I know today's a lot." No emoji. No request attached. Just the words, sitting there.

choices.label: Say it back, and mean it

outcomes.text: "So are you. Thank you for saying it." You read the thread twice. Then a third time, in the bathroom, with the door locked.

choices.label: Screenshot it for the hard days

outcomes.text: You save it in a photo album called "Proof." Next to it: the ultrasound, and a picture of a perfect nap.
"Nothing. I just meant it." You feel like a jerk, then a little less like one when they send a heart anyway.
"...The good spatula. But I still meant it." You laugh out loud in the cereal aisle. Fair trade.

title: "Where Did You Put It?"
text: Your partner texts: "Where did you put the daycare backpack?" The "you" is doing a lot of work. You put it in their car last night, so they could find it.

outcomes.text: You apologize for a thing you did correctly. "Found it, thanks!" Peace, purchased at full price.

choices.label: "Where YOU put it. In YOUR car."

outcomes.text: Capital letters. Two sets. It's satisfying in the exact way that makes the evening worse.
They find the backpack, then the ledger. They go quiet, then take two of your rows for the weekend without being asked.
The ledger shows they packed it the last three days. You found one backpack. They found the receipts.

title: The Empty Carton
text: The milk carton is in the fridge. It is empty. Someone put an empty carton back, and there are two suspects, and one of them can't reach the fridge.

choices.label: Let it go. Black coffee it is.

outcomes.text: You drink it black. You are an adult. You are, at most, 15% bitter about it, and the coffee is 85%.

choices.label: Text a photo of the carton. No caption.

outcomes.text: No caption needed. The photo says everything. Their reply, "lol sorry," says less.

choices.label: Open the ledger to the groceries column

outcomes.text: "...I'll get milk." They get milk. They also get the good cookies. An apology in snack form.
They reply with photos of the last four grocery receipts. All theirs. You drink the coffee black, as penance.

title: "Who Taught Them That?"
text: Your partner calls on speaker. The toddler grabs the phone and says "[BLEEP]" with crisp, professional diction. A pause. Then: "Who taught them that?"

outcomes.text: You confess. They laugh, then admit they said it in traffic on Sunday. A joint custody of the word.
"I don't swear in the car." You both know what happens at the merge onto the highway. Neither of you says so.

choices.label: Make a crackling noise. "You're breaking up!"

outcomes.text: "Krrrsh." It's not convincing. You hang up. The toddler says the word again, to the toaster.

title: Running 20 Late
text: "Running 20 late, sorry!!" Two exclamation points. You know what two exclamation points cost. You've sent them yourself.

outcomes.text: Two exclamation points back. The universal sign of a parent doing their best. Twenty minutes is forty, but you knew that.
The period lands like a dropped plate. They'll be home in twenty minutes, already apologizing.
They walk in with dumplings and a guilty face. You'd take this deal every night of the week.
They forget. They walk in with apologies and a work bag, and nothing that can be eaten.

title: Calendar Tetris
text: "Can you do pickup Thursday? I have a thing." Their Thursday thing is a work dinner. Your Thursday thing is pickup. All of your things are pickup.

outcomes.text: "You're the best." You are. It's on the calendar now, in your color, next to all your other things in your color.
"What thing?" You invent a dentist. You'll have to go to the dentist now. This is how lies work.
"Deal." They take bedtime tonight. You do Thursday. A fair trade, negotiated by two people who used to talk about books.
"Two? It's one pickup." Talks collapse. You get Thursday anyway, and a reputation as a hostage-taker.

title: The Dishwasher Doctrine
text: Your partner is reloading the dishwasher you just loaded. Silently. Correcting it. Every bowl they move is a small, wordless essay about you.

choices.label: Ask them to teach you their system

outcomes.text: They light up. There's a system. It has a philosophy. Bowls face the center, "like a congregation." You learn it. You'll never use it.

choices.label: "There's no wrong way to load a dishwasher."

outcomes.text: "There are many wrong ways. You found a new one." You leave the room. The bowls stay where they put them.

choices.label: Show them the dishes column of the ledger

outcomes.text: They look at the ledger, then at the bowl in their hand. They put the bowl back exactly where you had it.
The dishes column is mostly theirs. They keep loading. You go fold something, quietly, with dignity.

title: The Handoff: Running on Fumes
text: Your partner walks in and finds you lying on the kitchen floor while the toddler drives a toy truck up and down your back. "Hi," you tell the floor.

outcomes.text: They take the toddler. You take the stairs one at a time, like an old dog, and lie face-down on the bed. Ten minutes. Glorious.

choices.label: "I'm fine." Get up and start dinner.

outcomes.text: You are not fine. You make pasta anyway. They watch you salt the water three times and say nothing, which is its own kindness.

choices.label: Tell them the truth: you're running on fumes

outcomes.text: "I'm running on fumes." They sit down on the floor next to you. The toddler drives the truck over both of you. Nobody gets up for a while.

title: The Handoff: "I'm Wrecked."
text: Your partner walks in, drops their bag and says, "I'm wrecked." By your count you've done four more things than them this week. You have counted. You are always counting.

outcomes.text: You let the count go, for tonight. They sit. They look at you like you're someone they'd like to marry, which, technically, happened.

choices.label: Read them the count, out loud

outcomes.text: Mornings, dishes, the forms, the snack bag. They listen. They say "okay." The okay has a temperature, and it's cold.
They know the count too. They take the toddler without a word. You take a shower long enough to legally count as a bath.
They take the toddler with a sigh you'll hear in your dreams. You take the ten minutes anyway. They were owed. You think.
